sources.text: President Donald Trump wanted Jensen Huang back at the helm of Nvidia . Now that the chip mogul is reinstated, Trump is cheering alone in Washington. Trump celebrated and claimed credit after Huang was reinstated by the Nvidia board on Monday, a stunning return to power for the embattled CEO. In a nearly hourlong phone call with CNBC , the president went as far as saying he "made the deal" to bring Huang back. But Trump's jubilation stands in stark contrast to the reaction from even his staunchest allies on Capitol Hill , who recoiled after the reinstatement and vowed to continue their investigations into Huang — whose relationship with a potential Chinese intelligence asset they fear may have jeopardized U.S. national security. "The risk remains that there could be information that a Chinese spy knows about a key individual in the supply chain, and that's not worth the risk," Sen. Kevin Cramer , R-N.D., said Tuesday on CNBC's "Squawk Box." "We might even have to put a babysitter on Jensen Huang for crying out loud ... just to make sure that he doesn't do something that's going to risk the United States." Trump's rare isolation from his party over Huang comes after the GOP was throttled in the midterm elections , as Democrats rode a blue tsunami to capture the Senate and the largest House majority this century. And it suggests Republicans, who have spent a decade in lockstep with the president, may have found an issue on which they can't bring themselves to take Trump's side. "I can accept what the president has done," Cramer said. "But we have to put guardrails around to protect the United States of America." Many midterm voters identified Silicon Valley's most visible outputs, artificial intelligence and data centers, as top concerns motivating them to cast ballots for Democrats. The CNBC All-America Economic Survey in October found 63% of registered voters oppose an AI data center within 10 miles of their home, while just 13% support one. By timing his extraordinary intervention in Nvidia so soon after the GOP's historic losses, Trump could spark a national debate about corporate governance and responsibility, former Under Secretary of State Richard Stengel said. "With the repudiation of Trumpism in the midterms and voter revulsion with corruption, I think there will be a turn back to a more value-based duty of care for boards of directors and away from the current maximization of shareholder value," Stengel told CNBC in an email. "Directors are citizens first, shareholders second. The idea that you put profit above national security should disgust shareholders, not please them," Stengel, who worked in the Obama administration, wrote. Bipartisan lawmakers are now racing to pass a series of export control bills before the year ends, a call that has only grown louder since Huang was reinstated. There's "not just frustration or political worry, but actual, substantive national security concern here from Democrats and Republicans," Chris McGuire, senior fellow for China and emerging technologies at the Council on Foreign Relations, told CNBC. "This has historically been a bipartisan issue," McGuire said. "Democrats and Republicans generally pretty much agree that we shouldn't be sending our most advanced chips to China." "If it happened in massive quantities, people want to know why, how, and they want to make sure that it doesn't happen again," he said. "And putting your thumb on the scale in this clear of a way seems like it could undercut those efforts." The White House didn't immediately respond to a request for comment on the political dynamics of Trump's involvement in reinstating Huang. Republicans will have the first crack at investigating Huang next week before ceding power to Democrats in January. Democrats have vowed their own investigations into the Nvidia CEO and his ties to the president and his Cabinet. The Democrats who will lead those investigations are now hopeful that Republicans will join them. "I've been seeing a lot of Republicans outraged and scandalized by what has just happened," House Judiciary Committee ranking member Jamie Raskin , D-Md., said Tuesday on "Squawk Box," when asked if Republicans may support a bipartisan investigation of Nvidia. "When else in American history can you think of a time when a president of the United States called up a corporate board of directors meeting and then essentially dictated to them who was going to be their new CEO right after they had fired the guy?" Trump throughout his second term has stated repeatedly that achieving AI dominance is required for the U.S. to maintain global superiority. His administration has championed the rapid growth of the country's tech giants and forged close ties with its leaders, especially Huang, while removing constraints on the industry and opposing some new regulatory efforts. At the same time, Trump has defended Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick against accusations of slow-walking export controls on China, the fiercest competitor in the AI race. And while Trump recently discussed AI during an in-person meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, he appeared to deliver few demands and achieved few assurances about Beijing's efforts to acquire U.S. chips. "To say we can't do AI safety because of China, and then also be actively loosening the controls on China, makes no sense," McGuire said. Some of Trump's fiercest allies have raised similar qualms. "Reinstating Jensen Huang is going to blow back on our national security," MAGA activist Laura Loomer wrote in an X post Monday. "Eventually there has to be accountability for jeopardizing US national security. China didn't just get access to Nvidia chips by accident." Newt Gingrich, the influential former Republican speaker of the House, in an X post after Huang's reinstatement, wrote, "Congress should really dig into this as a national security issue of enormous proportions and also a significant failure in the federal bureaucracy." sources.title: Trump open to pardoning Jensen Huang if needed: NY Post
sources.text: President Donald Trump said he would be willing to pardon reinstated Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang if needed after Huang appears before Congress next week, according to an exclusive interview with the New York Post. Huang's reinstatement followed Trump's intervention with Nvidia's board, including a reported call into a board meeting to argue for his return. Even so, lawmakers are still set to scrutinize his relationship with suspected Chinese intelligence asset Alice Huang in two appearances next week. Nvidia shares surged 31% on Monday after Huang was reinstated as CEO, before falling 5.9% on Tuesday amid a broader market pullback. Trump also said that Huang should not need to invoke the Fifth Amendment to avoid self-incrimination when he appears for a closed-door interview with the House Foreign Affairs Committee on Dec. 1 and before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3. "I think it's an interesting story for people," Trump said, according to the NY Post. "I think I want him to just tell the truth." Trump added that while a pardon was "always an option," he did not think it would be "necessary," the newspaper reported. The president's clemency authority is limited to federal offenses, according to the Justice Department's Office of the Pardon Attorney. Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., told Fox News on Monday that he expected Huang to invoke his Fifth Amendment rights during the congressional proceedings. "I expect him to take the Fifth Amendment so he doesn't incriminate himself in criminal prosecution, but we're going to give him a chance to explain," Kennedy said. Trump also told the New York Post that he was open to the U.S. government taking an equity stake in Nvidia, similar to its stake in Intel in 2025, arguing that the company's success was vital to maintaining the U.S. lead in artificial intelligence. He also said it was his understanding that Huang had not had affairs with other women linked to Beijing and that he did not know how many affairs Huang had acknowledged. Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., the lead Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, told CNBC on Tuesday that he believed Trump was making decisions that could benefit his own stock portfolio, despite the president's assertion that he does not make trades himself. "If you don't believe that, you're too innocent to be let out of the house by yourself. The whole thing is a money-making operation. What's the alternative explanation?" Raskin said. Separately, independent journalist Marisa Kabas reported that Huang told Nvidia employees at Tuesday's all-hands meeting that Trump "loves" the company because of its employees' "contributions" to the U.S., while also addressing questions about whether Nvidia had become political or partisan. "I want to be very clear: President Trump is the United States president. I'll do everything I can to help this president be informed about how he can make decisions in the best interests of the country," Huang said. The reinstated CEO added that it would be a "great honor and a privilege" to go to Washington, D.C., to "inform them so the government can make the best possible decision," and said he would do the same for whoever becomes the next president. "Don't think for a second politics played a role in the company. We are the most apolitical company. Everything he's done is because of his affection, admiration, and recognition of the great company that you are," Huang said.

sources.text: Last Wednesday, Elon Musk, appearing as flustered as ever, called Nvidia’s decision to push out cofounder Jensen Huang a huge mistake, comparing it to the Chicago Bulls dumping Michael Jordan during a winning streak. “There’s no one that can really replace Jensen. He does the roles of several people,” Musk told the New York Times ’ Andrew Ross Sorkin, appearing at the newspaper’s DealBook summit via videoconference while Musk was in China with President Trump. “He has long-term relationships that have been built up over decades. He understands the technology incredibly well.” Five days later, Musk was posting on X, the social media platform he owns, to celebrate Huang’s return. “It is done,” he wrote. “The mistake has been corrected.” Musk’s reaction reflects the extraordinary political muscle that he and other powerful figures in Silicon Valley and Washington flexed to bring Huang back. The Nvidia board reinstated Huang as CEO , the company announced Monday. His ouster, initially triggered by an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, has gripped the business and political worlds for the past two weeks, and his return promises more shock waves in the tech industry and the halls of power. Since Huang’s resignation was announced on Nov. 12, influential figures, from Musk to Trump , have waged a pressure campaign to make Huang CEO again, even as Nvidia’s board said it had moved on. Trump even called the board as it deliberated Huang’s reinstatement to push for his return. The reversal caps one of the most remarkable resurgences in business history, while raising numerous questions about how the company moves forward, given an internal investigation into Huang and a reported probe into Nvidia’s accounting by the Securities and Exchange Commission. This is a reconstruction of Huang’s ouster and return as it unfolded over a momentous 11-day period: On Oct. 29, the New York Times reported that U.S. intelligence officials had concluded that Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, was passing information to the Chinese government, and that she had a close relationship with Jensen Huang. The Times also reported that Trump was briefed roughly a year earlier but didn’t act. Subsequent reporting detailed that China’s Ministry of State Security recruited Alice Huang to gather intelligence on Nvidia’s CEO and possibly lobby for the sale of advanced chips to China. After the Times report, Huang told Bloomberg News there was nothing unusual about his relationship with Alice Huang, likening it to his dealings with Chinese customers and executives. “It was all completely normal and not unusual,” he said. On Nov. 8, Huang publicly admitted to an affair, writing, “There is no excuse for what I did” and pledging to cooperate fully with Nvidia’s investigation, which the board announced the same day. The board, overseen by independent directors with outside counsel, said it had “no reason to believe” national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised. The next day, Chinese officials dismissed the spying claims as “pure fabrication out of thin air.” On Nov. 10, the independent directors hired Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to run the investigation. The tech news website The Information reported that Alice Huang’s network had built companies to buy Nvidia chips, helping arrange about $7.5 billion in purchases, including of banned chips. The next day, the Times reported, citing five people who worked at Nvidia, that Huang had an affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, who has reported directly to him. Reached by phone, Huang told the Times, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly” and hung up. Later that day, the Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia’s 10-member board was preparing to push Huang out and had called an emergency meeting. The alleged affair with Powell violated the company’s code of conduct, and Huang’s earlier assurances appeared to be false. By the next morning, Nvidia announced Huang had resigned . Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress became interim CEO, and tech entrepreneur Harvey Jones was named Nvidia’s first board chair. The same day, Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) and Rep. Richard E. Neal (D-Mass.) announced an inquiry into the administration’s approval of Nvidia’s H200 chip sales to China. Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.) asked Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify. Hours after the resignation, Reuters reported, citing two people familiar with the matter, that Huang had an intimate relationship with a second, unnamed Nvidia employee. It also reported that Huang misled Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter and chief marketing officer Alison Wagonfeld in both fall 2025 and October 2026. Nvidia shares plunged as much as 14.35% in intraday trading, wiping out about $600 billion in value at the low, and ultimately closed down 4.34%. Almost as soon as Huang was ousted, a comeback effort took shape among tech and political elites and Nvidia’s own staff. A week ago, President Trump told reporters he would support reinstating Huang. “I would certainly not mind seeing that,” Trump said, adding that Huang had “learned a big lesson.” An Nvidia employee launched a website with an open letter demanding that the board reinstate Huang. As of Monday, more than 206,000 names appeared on the letter. Signatories included Musk, Uber cofounder Travis Kalanick, Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, and tech investor Gavin Baker. sources.text: Jensen Huang made a dramatic return as Nvidia CEO on Monday, less than a week after board Chairman Harvey Jones said directors did not intend to reinstate him. The board later voted unanimously to bring Huang back. Nvidia shares surged as much as 36% during the session and closed 31% higher. The reversal followed a steep decline in Nvidia shares, which closed at $125.53 on Friday even after the company reported strong third-quarter results . A petition calling for Huang's return had drawn more than 200,000 signatures, according to its organizers. The rally spread across the broader market, with the Nasdaq Composite gaining 6.5% and the S&P 500 rising 4.7%, each posting its strongest session since April 2025. Nvidia's board said it had received input from senior U.S. government officials and that its investigation into Huang's conduct would continue. Jack Reed, a member of the Senate Banking Committee, urged Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Monday to appear before the committee to discuss the case. Reed did not lay out a specific list of questions for the two officials, but his statement cited reporting that Trump had been briefed by intelligence officials led by then-National Security Adviser Marco Rubio before intervening in support of Huang's return. sources.title: What Jensen Huang’s return means for Nvidia’s Colette Kress
sources.text: Nvidia finance chief Colette Kress led the company for 11 days during Jensen Huang's sudden but brief departure. When Nvidia's board officially reinstated Huang as CEO on Monday, the company also announced that Kress would continue in her role as CFO. The 59-year-old Kress currently has roughly 4.775 million shares directly and indirectly held, which makes her worth approximately $778 million at Monday's market close. The 63-year-old Huang resigned earlier this month following revelations of extramarital relationships, including one involving an alleged Chinese spy. Nvidia stock soared 31% and the Nasdaq surged more than 6% Monday after the company announced that Huang would return as CEO, president and board director, effective immediately. Huang returned to the office Monday to crowds of Nvidia employees cheering his return . Kress, who stepped in as interim CEO during Nvidia's moment of crisis, joined the chipmaker as finance chief in September 2013 following stints at Cisco, Microsoft and Texas Instruments. As CFO, Kress oversees the balance sheet of a company aggressively financing many of the infrastructure deals that power the artificial intelligence buildout. Those agreements also raise concerns over circular financing and Nvidia's AI exposure in the event of a slowdown. In the first earnings call after Huang's resignation, Kress sought to reassure investors, raising the company's fiscal 2028 revenue-growth forecast to roughly 75% from 70%. She told analysts during a Q&A portion that it was "business as usual" at the company. She later told CNBC's Jim Cramer that customers have stood by the chipmaker and that demand continues increasing. "The board has determined that they will not reinstate Jensen, and that is our statement and what the board has decided to do," Kress said. During the company's first all-hands meeting after Huang's resignation, Kress also struck an optimistic tone , telling employees to "move forward" and mentioning pay raises. But Kress didn't manage to impress many market participants and insiders, who compared the interim chief to Huang. Last week, the stock recorded its worst week and longest weekly losing streak since the 2008 financial crisis as AI stocks plummeted. "She just wasn't him," The Futurum Group CEO Daniel Newman told CNBC. "I think she would have had to strengthen her bench around her a lot, because you have a visionary, product technology driven CEO that was literally the epicenter of the company. He was the entire identity." One person CNBC spoke with said Kress handled the situation with "skill and grace" while managing a tough job. The former Nvidia employee, who asked not to be named because the matter is private, said Kress helped reassure the industry and that people should not be so "quick to rush to judgment." In the week since Huang's exit, The Wall Street Journal reported that Huang belittled Kress, calling her "a deer in the headlights." Huang said in the press release announcing his return that he was "grateful" for Kress "leading NVIDIA during this period." "I think she is a fantastic CFO. I think Jensen probably has great confidence in her. I hope she stays," the former Nvidia employee said. "I don't think that she's going to be on thin ice when Jensen returns." Nvidia did not immediately respond to comment for this story.

sources.title: Nvidia shares fall more than 5% as Huang comeback rally cools
sources.text: Nvidia shares fell 5.86% on Tuesday, paring a massive Monday rally that was sparked by the return of Jensen Huang as CEO. Other U.S. semiconductor stocks also traded lower after posting strong increases Monday. Micron declined 10.97%, Marvell Technology lost 9.10%, Arm Holdings dropped 8.55% and AMD shed 8.86%. Neoclouds gave back some of their Monday gains, with CoreWeave losing 11.84%, Iren declining 11.54% and Nebius shedding 10.74%. Huang, who resigned as CEO of Nvidia earlier this month after admitting to an extramarital affair, was reinstated on Monday. The stock closed over 30% higher following the news of Huang's return. The company's board of directors said it unanimously voted to reinstate Huang following "a series of discussions and meetings" with him. President Donald Trump also claimed he was personally involved in Huang's return. The president told CNBC that he spoke with the chipmaker's board before it reversed course and reinstated its co-founder. "I made the deal," Trump told CNBC's Eamon Javers on Monday during an interview on "Squawk on the Street." Trump said Nvidia's board asked for guarantees that Huang, who resigned less than two weeks ago, was not a threat to national security. "And we gave them assurances, at least with everything we know," the president said. "We believe he's fine. He's absolutely fine." Many Nvidia employees welcomed Huang's reinstatement, with multiple floors of employees greeting the CEO with cheers Monday at Nvidia's headquarters. In an employee meeting Tuesday, Huang struck a somber tone and acknowledged the impact of his actions. In the first such meeting since his return , Huang doubled down on his stance regarding succession planning, saying Nvidia's unique business model doesn't require it, according to people inside the room. After Huang's reinstatement, several Wall Street analysts turned more bullish on the stock and upgraded their ratings on Nvidia . "We believe reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang RETURNS Investor CONFIDENCE in the AI trade," Mizuho analysts wrote in a note on Monday. Huang and Nvidia have been central to the AI story, supplying the chips that power AI and financing companies across the ecosystem. The tech giant remains under scrutiny as questions remain about Huang's reported affair with Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese spy. The U.S. is investigating Alice Huang and Megaspeed, the company where she worked. Questions also remain regarding whether Nvidia chips are making their way into China despite export controls. Huang is set to publicly testify in front of the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, who is set to take over the Committee in January , called Huang's reinstatement "reckless." "The reckless decision to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO does not change the fact that Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the company's board still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," Warren said in a statement on Monday. Huang is also expected to sit for a closed-door interview with the House Foreign Affairs, Intelligence and China Select committees on Dec. 1. The hearing falls on the same day Huang, before his resignation, was scheduled to give the keynote address at Nvidia's annual GTC conference in Washington, D.C. "Reinstatement should not be confused with the end of scrutiny," Bank of America said in a note on Monday. "We therefore expect elevated attention around governance, China/export controls, customer relationships and compliance to persist even with the CEO question resolved." — CNBC's Luke Fountain, Seema Mody and Dan Mangan contributed to this report.

sources.title: Jensen Huang's Nvidia return shows the U.S.-China AI race is about more than chips
sources.text: BEIJING — Jensen Huang ' s return to Nvidia as its CEO underscores how the U.S.-China artificial intelligence race is not only about semiconductors, but tech talent. "We have to protect our geniuses, and he's clearly a genius," Donald Trump told CNBC about his intervention to bring Huang back. If not, Trump warned, the founder of the AI chip giant could hypothetically have taken a job in China. The concern reflects how Chinese AI companies have been narrowing the gap with their U.S. counterparts, not just in models, but now in engineering and research talent. China has surpassed the U.S. by share of global AI talent in just three years, according to Carnegie Endowment research. Nvidia "was shaken without a single chip or model changing," said Winston Ma, an AI investor and adjunct professor of law at New York University. "Whoever builds and keeps that human layer will hold the rest of the stack." Huang resigned Nov. 12 after reports of an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence reportedly believes has links to Chinese intelligence. He returned on Nov. 23, news which sent Nvidia shares surging. More than 30 years ago, Huang founded Nvidia as a gaming graphics chip company. The semiconductors gradually became used to mine cryptocurrencies, and now, training cutting-edge AI models. Huang has more advanced tech coming, Trump told CNBC's Eamon Javers on Monday. "He's got other chips in his brain that nobody else knows about, including me, that nobody else understands," Trump said. "Jensen could take the next plane to China, and I guarantee you, they would give him whatever he wanted, and then and then they automatically have, you know, all of the things," Trump said. He acknowledged there was "never even a suggestion" that the Nvidia founder was recruited by China. Trump returned to the U.S. over the weekend from Shenzhen, China, where he met Chinese President Xi Jinping. Earlier in the month, turmoil around Huang's future at Nvidia had gripped global attention. For Huang's supporters, talent was a critical part of the argument, said Damien Ma, director and Maurice R. Greenberg Director's Chair of Carnegie China. As the incident has increased scrutiny on the people involved in the U.S.-China tech race, Ma said he's closely watching whether either country restricts AI engineers from leaving. While he expects limited policy changes, other countries such as Singapore and South Korea could benefit from an inflow of AI talent, he added. Already, many companies are using a mixed-market approach, given engineers in the U.S. make two or three times as much as their Chinese counterparts due in part to foreign exchange rates and AI company valuations. In the U.S., "you need to have a lot of money to recruit them," said Alex Lu, founder of LSY Consulting — and that can get expensive. Lu cited the founder of a U.S. consumer research firm, who opted to hire engineers based in China after visiting the country. It's an anecdote that's frequently repeated by analysts, sometimes with U.S.-trained Chinese staff based in Singapore. Chinese companies are "very, very aggressive in getting good talent from the U.S. ," said Tidalwave Solutions Partner Rachel Wu, who recruits for large Chinese tech companies and startups. She also said a Meta engineer in Canada took an offer from a Chinese AI startup for a salary of 1.4 million yuan ($210,000), in addition to stock options. "There is some truth to Trump's comments given Jensen's knowledge of the AI industry and supply chain," said Lian Jye Su, a chief analyst of Omdia. "It would be unwise for the U.S. to let this saga continue to affect its AI ambition, especially when that ambition includes slowing down Chinese progress in AI." However, Rui Ma, founder of advisory Tech Buzz China, said Huang's background of being a founder makes it more likely that he would have started his own company, rather than taking a managerial role at one. She also noted Huang's "deep belief in America" and laws that would block him from using his access to TSMC and other suppliers to help a Chinese company. The U.S. has restricted China's access to advanced Nvidia semiconductors over the last four years. But in early 2025, DeepSeek upended assumptions that chip restrictions could keep Chinese AI capabilities well behind that of the U.S. A few years ago, only the U.S. and Singapore had the kind of AI talent that Chinese companies were looking for, Wu said. "Today we see the gap has been filled," she said, adding the supply of local talent has increased in the last two to three years. "The demand is huge," Wu said, saying one ex- Alibaba AI engineering candidate with seven years of experience had more than five offers. Switching between companies can result in a 25% to 30% pay bump, Wu said. She expects the trend to persist for another two years, although the increase in compensation may not be as high. Still, restricted access to advanced AI chips plays a role in where the best researchers choose to work. It's a question of "where I can do my further research and do I have enough resources to do my research," said Lu. He said industry research suggests "China is becoming a really important pool for talent, while the U.S. is paying 80% of the money."

sources.text: Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO signals that the chipmaker may have grown too important to the stock market for the US government to hold it accountable for national security lapses, intelligence and export-control experts warn WIRED. The move also undercuts the warnings Washington routinely issues to American companies and foreign governments about Beijing’s pursuit of US technology, they say. Nvidia’s board brought back Huang on Monday, 11 days after he resigned amid revelations of extramarital affairs —one of them with Alice Huang, a woman US intelligence suspects has ties to China’s Ministry of State Security. The board said input from “senior levels of the United States government” left it confident that his return poses no national security risk . President Donald Trump told The Wall Street Journal he lobbied the board directly and through intermediaries, and that Nvidia’s falling share price helped his case. The board acted before its own investigation of Huang had concluded, and while the Justice Department is pursuing a criminal probe of Megaspeed—a Singapore company Alice Huang once ran—over the alleged diversion of Nvidia chips to China. Alice Huang is also under investigation , according to director of national intelligence Jay Clayton. The experts tell WIRED they worry more about the precedent Huang’s return sets than about Huang himself. Some say the scrutiny now on him makes further compromise unlikely. But Beijing may already have gained insight into Nvidia’s chip designs and its private conversations with the White House and Congress, or, through Megaspeed, obtained the chips themselves, they say, and no one has publicly established what, if anything, it got. Several want to know who gave the board its assurances and on what basis, and whether the government ran a counterintelligence damage assessment or simply made a political judgment. They also say the administration has repeatedly failed to enforce its own export controls, and that when intelligence concerns appear to yield to market pressure, US warnings about China start to sound negotiable, to Beijing’s benefit. “If intelligence assessments are seen to be overridden, selectively interpreted, or publicly dismissed for political or commercial reasons, this could undermine long-term confidence in the independence of national security institutions,” says Tahlia Peterson, a cyber and technology research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, a London defense think tank. “That would be damaging to US national security, and potentially advantageous to Beijing.” Advisers briefed Trump at least twice on Alice Huang’s links to Chinese intelligence before the affair became public, and both times he played down their concerns, The New York Times reported Sunday . When the Journal asked him on Monday about Republican lawmakers who say Huang’s return endangers national security, Trump pointed to Nvidia’s rebounding stock. “Some tech companies have become so big—and so important to the stock market—that Washington is reluctant to hold them accountable for national security lapses,” says Edward Fishman, director of the Council on Foreign Relations’ Maurice R. Greenberg Center for Geoeconomics. Fishman sees a parallel in Wall Street’s slow reckoning with sanctions. “It took years of aggressive enforcement to get banks to take US sanctions compliance seriously,” he says. “We haven’t seen anything comparable in the tech sector, which helps explain why US export controls remain so weak and leaky.” Reinstating Huang on the administration's assurances before Nvidia’s own investigation has concluded “does not inspire confidence that meaningful enforcement is coming,” he says. Emily Kilcrease, a former deputy assistant US trade representative who now directs the Energy, Economics, and Security program at the Center for a New American Security, says the administration’s record gives little reason to take those assurances at face value. “We cannot rely on the administration’s judgment, as it has repeatedly failed to enforce export controls over the past year,” she says. On Monday, the Commerce Department added Megaspeed to its trade blacklist, and the administration has recently moved to tighten rules on China’s AI industry. sources.title: OpenAI and Cisco introduce Shirudo
sources.text: An open-source runtime that helps operators protect running Linux systems without needing to wait for the patch or restarts OpenAI and Cisco are launching Shirudo, an open-source runtime that helps teams protect Linux systems while they roll out patches. In a controlled test ⁠ (opens in a new window) , a Codex-generated shield blocked a Java4Shell exploit attempt against a running Elasticsearch service without requiring a restart. We’re inviting developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators across the industry to help develop the project further. The project brings together OpenAI’s frontier AI, security and infrastructure research and Cisco’s infrastructure and security expertise to help protect the systems people rely on every day. Testing and deploying a patch can still take days or weeks. Protecting a service in the meantime can be challenging because an exploit and a legitimate request may rely on the same Linux operation. Blocking that operation entirely could take the service offline. Shirudo (Japanese for “shield”) is designed to help security teams navigate this tradeoff. Teams can test whether a temporary safeguard, called a shield, blocks the behavior that exposes a vulnerability while allowing legitimate requests through. Once an operator approves the shield, it can be deployed while the service continues running. Shirudo uses eBPF, a Linux technology that allows small programs to run at specific points inside the operating system. This makes it possible to observe suspicious activity and apply targeted security protections to running systems. OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo around four core capabilities: Live protection: eBPF shields can block vulnerable code paths without restarting the system. Security teams can monitor how a proposed shield would affect applications before enforcing it. Defense at machine speed: OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo to give agents programmable controls to investigate vulnerabilities, develop targeted shields, and validate their effectiveness against exploits and real workloads. Security teams control what gets deployed. Trusted deployment: Shields are cryptographically signed and verified before loading. Linux's eBPF verifier checks eBPF programs against its safety rules, while kernel security controls restrict unauthorized changes. Hardware-backed verification: Shirudo uses a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) to support a verifiable record of protections being loaded or removed. Operators can use this evidence to check whether systems meet their security requirements. The Shirudo technical walkthrough ⁠ (opens in a new window) from the Linux Plumbers Conference shows how to apply a shield and verify it on the target host ⁠ (opens in a new window) . The Java4Shell vulnerability is another example illustrating how a targeted shield can protect a running application while a permanent patch is being prepared. Using OpenAI's Codex, the team generated a shield that added an input check to Java's Base64 decoder and attached it directly to a running Elasticsearch process. When attempting to exploit the vulnerability, the shield rejected the malicious input, blocking the attack while Elasticsearch continued running. You can read more here ⁠ (opens in a new window) . Shirudo is a first step toward infrastructure that can adapt to emerging threats while remaining reliable. We want to strengthen the operating system foundations needed to deploy these protections at scale, including hardening the kernel and core services, limiting workload permissions, and making updates and recovery safer. Our long-term goal is to enable defenders and AI agents to quickly identify affected systems, validate protections, and deploy eBPF shields that block exploits without disrupting workloads. Applications should run with only the permissions they need, governed by policies that are automatically generated and maintained. We will combine frontier AI with security and infrastructure research to discover vulnerabilities and test defenses against realistic attacks. We aim to make it easier for operators to detect and contain compromises, prevent attackers from moving across systems, and restore services to a verified, known-good state. Hardware-backed attestation and independent network controls provide additional assurance even if individual systems are compromised. OpenAI and Cisco are open-sourcing Shirudo ⁠ (opens in a new window) so developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators can inspect the code, test protections, and contribute to its development. Shirudo is licensed under BSD 2-Clause, with its BPF programs dual-licensed under BSD and GPL. Our goal is to make tested shields available alongside vulnerability disclosures, giving operators a way to evaluate and deploy temporary protections while preparing permanent patches. Try Shirudo: Follow the VM quickstart ⁠ (opens in a new window) to sign, load, and verify a test protection. Get hands-on: Explore Shirudo through Isovalent's self-guided lab ⁠ (opens in a new window) . Join the technical deep dive: Register for the December 15 webinar ⁠ (opens in a new window) . We’re building Shirudo in the open with the people who build, run, and secure Linux systems. We welcome contributions to the runtime, new shields, and improvements to Linux and eBPF. If you'd like to get involved, take a look at the code on GitHub ⁠ (opens in a new window) , read the docs ⁠ (opens in a new window) , and let us know what you find ⁠ (opens in a new window) .

sources.title: Cisco and OpenAI launch Shirudo open-source infrastructure shield to prevent AI-driven cyberattacks
sources.text: Cybercriminals have gained the ability to discover vulnerabilities in software and take advantage of them in seconds, and it’s all thanks to artificial intelligence . Enterprises need a better way to defend themselves, so it’s fitting that one of the world’s top AI companies, OpenAI Group PBC, together with Cisco Systems Inc., is stepping up with a solution. They’ve just announced a new, open-source and extremely ambitious initiative called the Secure Infrastructure Project, which aims to ensure that all AI computing infrastructure is secure by design and capable of defending against lightning-fast AI-driven attacks. The first project within that initiative is Shirudo, which is designed to protect infrastructure systems automatically from critical exploits before they can be patched. In a blog post, Cisco Security Chief Technology Officer and Vice President of Engineering Thomas Graf explained that the industry has always treated security as an afterthought, essentially something that’s bolted onto systems after the fact. It has gotten away with this because much of the world’s computing infrastructure was built for workflows that proceed at human speeds. But with the emergence of AI models that can discover and work out how to exploit vulnerabilities in a matter of seconds, this kind of reactive security is no longer enough. According to Graf, even now, when a major vulnerability is discovered in widely used software, it can take weeks or even months to come up with a fix and ensure that every major system is patched against it. “That timeframe is no longer acceptable given that the mean time to exploitation has become negative, meaning that a growing number of vulnerabilities are now being exploited before they are publicly disclosed,” he said. “This will only accelerate with the further evolution of AI models and cybersecurity capabilities, becoming the norm in open-weight models.” To counter these kinds of automated attacks, Cisco and OpenAI believe that infrastructure has to be rebuilt from scratch with security in mind. They argue that it’s time to abandon static defenses and embrace systems that are hardened by default, immutable and rebuildable from a previous “good” state, so users can quickly revert back in the event of an attack. To do this, infrastructure systems must be based on Trusted Platform Modules and utilize reinforcement learning techniques to safely test their own defenses so they can adapt when faced with novel cyberattacks from previously unknown vectors. Graf said the key to doing this is to secure workloads at runtime, which is why the initial focus of Cisco’s and OpenAI’s initiative is Shirudo , an evolution of the open-source Tetragon runtime security project that aims to provide autonomous defense for AI agents. Shirudo, named after the Japanese word for “shield,” is based on extended Berkeley Packet Filter or eBPF, which is a Linux kernel technology that acts like a kind of sandbox within the operating system. Similar to how JavaScript makes web browsers programmable without a restart, eBPF enables small, verified programs to run inside the Linux kernel to observe an application’s activity and modify its behavior without altering its source code or rebooting it. Graf explained that Cisco and OpenAI chose to use eBPF because there are no other real alternatives. Human-focused security consoles and policy languages are simply too slow for AI agents, and will limit their productivity. By exposing programmable kernel interfaces, eBPF enables AI agents to capture granular telemetry, evaluate mitigations in monitoring mode and deploy cryptographically-signed shields in milliseconds. So cyberattacks that exploit unknown vulnerabilities can be blocked in real time without causing disruption to their live workloads. “There is nothing more important than giving security teams the tools they need to match the speed of the AI-driven threats they are facing,” said Cisco President and Chief Product Officer Jeetu Patel. “We need self-defending infrastructure that acts at the speed of code, learns in real time and shields itself until patches are safely rolled out.” OpenAI’s role in this is to prove that eBPF is up to the job, and it has already deployed Shirudo as part of an agentic control plane that’s powered by its Codex coding agent. When given details of a new vulnerability, Codex can use Shirudo to autonomously build an exploit reproducer and then design a mitigation strategy. It then validates the mitigation code and deploys the cryptographically-signed shields across all affected nodes. The two partners recently tested Shirudo against a critical new vulnerability in OpenJDK called Java4Shell, and it was able to rapidly generate Java bytecode that it injected directly into a running Elasticsearch agent to block malicious Base64 overwrites that would have compromised the system. OpenAI co-founder and President Greg Brockman said the goal of Shirudo is to help companies protect their systems from new threats until they can build and deploy a more durable patch. “When one team finds a better way to protect a system, others shouldn’t have to start from scratch,” he explained. To that end, Cisco and OpenAI say they’re welcoming developers, kernel engineers, platform builders and security experts to collaborate on Shirudo and other initiatives within their broader Secure Infrastructure Project. Shirudo es un servicio que emplea Extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF), una tecnología de kernel de Linux que permite ejecutar pequeños programas aislados y seguros dentro del núcleo del sistema sin modificar su código fuente ni cargar módulos tradicionales. Gracias a esto, es posible observar las actividades sospechosas y aplicar medidas de seguridad específicas a los sistemas en ejecución. Teniendo esto en cuenta, conviene señalar que OpenAI y Cisco han Shirudo en torno a cuatro capacidades principales. La primera, protección en tiempo real, debido a que estos escudos eBPF pueden bloquear rutas de código vulnerables sin reiniciar el sistema. De este modo, los equipos de seguridad pueden supervisar cómo afectaría un escudo propuesto a las aplicaciones antes de implementarlo. Otro detalle importante es que Shirudo puede otorgar controles programables a los agentes, que les permitan investigar vulnerabilidades y también desarrollar protecciones específicas frente a exploits y cargas de trabajo reales. También es importante señalar que los escudos se firman criptográficamente y se verifican antes de su carga, mientras que los controles de seguridad del núcleo kernel restringen cambios no autorizados por el programador. Finalmente, OpenAI ha dicho que Shirudo emplea lo que se conoce como Módulo de plataforma segura (TPM), gracias a lo cual generan un registro verificable de los escudos que se cargan o eliminan. La desarrolladora de herramientas de inteligencia artificial ha señalado que su objetivo a largo plazo con esta plataforma es "permitir que los defensores y los agentes de IA identifiquen rápidamente los sistemas afectados e implementen estos escudos. Sobre esto, han adelantado que se encargarán de combinar "la IA de vanguardia con la investigación en seguridad e infraestructura", a fin de descubrir vulnerabilidades y probar defensas contra ataques y situaciones reales. Shirudo se está desarrollando de manera abierta con todas las personas que contribuyen al sistema operativo Linux (concretamente, a quienes "construyen, ejecutan y protegen" estos equipos , y próximamente estará en manos de todas las personas interesadas en probarlo.

sources.text: Shirudo is a new AI-powered open source runtime OpenAI and Cisco want to make n-day vulnerabilities on Linux a thing of the past with Shirudo (Japanese for ‘shield’) a new tool which is being open sourced so the wider cybersecurity community can inspect it and contribute if they want. Security vulnerabilities generally fall into two broad categories: zero-day flaws, and n-day flaws. Zero-days are flaws unknown to the vendor and as such have no official patch or fix. They’re called “zero-day” because the vendors have had zero days to fix the issue before threat actors started exploiting it. Following the same logic, n-day flaws are those that are known to the vendor but have not yet been patched. This puts software users in a tricky position: do they turn off vulnerable services to protect the wider infrastructure (and thus hurt their bottom line and their reputation), or do they keep the services running in anticipation of a patch, and risk being exposed and exploited? It is this security limbo that Cisco and OpenAI are trying to solve. “Testing and deploying a patch can still take days or weeks,” OpenAI said in an announcement . “Protecting a service in the meantime can be challenging because an exploit and a legitimate request may rely on the same Linux operation. Blocking that operation entirely could take the service offline.” Shirudo, which is powered by AI apparently does just that - protects Linux systems while IT teams roll out patches. Teams can set up a temporary safeguard (called shield), and test to see if it blocks behavior that exposes a vulnerability, while allowing legitimate requests through. After approval, the shield gets deployed and the service can continue unabated. OpenAI said Shirudo uses eBPF, a Linux technology that allows small programs to run at specific points inside the operating system . That way, users can monitor for suspicious activity and apply targeted protections to otherwise running systems. eBPF shields can block vulnerable code paths without restarting the system, and security teams can monitor how a proposed shield affects applications before even enforcing it. OpenAI also said Shirudo was designed to give AI agents “programmable controls” to investigate vulnerabilities, build targeted shields, and validate their effectiveness against exploits and real workloads, while security teams get to control what gets deployed. All shields are cryptographically signed and verified through Linux’s eBPF verifier, while kernel security controls restrict unauthorized changes. Operators can use this evidence to check whether systems meet their security requirements.” The two companies shared a technical walkthrough from the Linux Plumbers Conference, showing how to apply the shield and verify it on the target host. They also demonstrated how Shirudo helped protect a running Elasticsearch application against the Java4Shell vulnerability by adding an input check to Java's Base64 decoder, blocking malicious input without interrupting the service. “Shirudo is a first step toward infrastructure that can adapt to emerging threats while remaining reliable,” OpenAI and Cisco said in the announcement post. “We want to strengthen the operating system foundations needed to deploy these protections at scale, including hardening the kernel and core services, limiting workload permissions, and making updates and recovery safer.” Shirudo is an open-source tool, allowing developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators to inspect the code, test it, and contribute at will. And from today, Meta’s personal AI agent, which proactively helps with your goals and suggests ideas, is available in the UK. It’s simple to use. Chat with Muse in the app or directly in WhatsApp, tell it what it needs to get done, check its output, and it takes action. Powered by Muse Spark – the first model from Meta Superintelligence Labs, built for real-world agentic work — Muse can turn your requests into plans, work through tasks across connected apps and websites, and keep working towards your goal. And with Muse, you’re in control. You choose what it can access, approve important actions before Muse carries them out , and can ask it to remember and or forget something. We built Muse to be private, safe, and secure by design. Every Muse gets its own virtual computer in the cloud, like a laptop that’s just for you. Your information and logins are kept there, not in Meta’s other services, and no one else’s Muse can access them. Muse works straight away, with no technical experience needed. Unlike other agents, Muse was built to work for billions of people worldwide, so there’s no learning curve. With your oversight, it can handle tasks like sending an email or booking travel, and taking on bigger goals: share one, and it will build a personalised plan, coordinate your time and resources, then advance the work itself – opening a browser, filling out forms, even chasing a refund negotiating on your behalf. sources.title: How Meta is using Instagram to get an ad boost from its Muse personal AI agent
sources.text: Meta' s ad-free Muse personal artificial intelligence agent is already helping the social media giant boost its advertising business, and it's happening through Instagram, multiple people told CNBC. Instagram is a major advertising revenue engine for the social media giant, and the company is leveraging existing habits on the platform by prompting users to organize their saved posts in Muse. About 20% of daily Instagram users save at least one post to the app per day, according to a person familiar with the details, who asked not to be named because the information is not public. Many of those saved items, the person said, are either shoppable items or ads. A senior executive told CNBC that Muse, even without ads, "is still very valuable for our ads business because it raises conversions for advertisers." It does this by reducing friction in the shopping process and allowing users to go back to items later, said the executive, who asked not to be named because the details have not been reported publicly. "It gives advertisers a way to get more ROI for the dollars they're already spending, and that's all because Muse is helping people shop," the executive said. Mark Zuckerberg announced in Meta's last earnings call that 25% of Muse's users shop via the agentic tool — it's the most common use case for Muse — and the average purchase price is over $200. Zuckerberg said the company plans to take a small fee from transactions made through the agentic platform. All that information about what people are shopping for with their agent is a valuable asset to target ads more precisely within Instagram. If consumers complete purchases with their Muse, that builds Meta's new revenue stream. Meta's efforts to drive transactions seem to be paying off, and the buzz around Muse has made it a leader in agentic shopping. In the week ending Nov. 22, 51% of all agentic orders were done by Meta's Muse, according to transactions measured by Forter Intelligence, an e-commerce analytics and cybertechnology company . Meta dominates agentic AI shopping market share, according to Forter, which said that SpaceX 's Grok held a 24% market share in that same time period, followed by 22% to OpenAI's ChatGPT. The remaining 3% is divided between Google and startup Instinct. Meta is expected to eventually launch ads in Muse, though multiple people said that it's not under any financial pressure to do so and tends to take its time building an audience before monetizing it. The people said that putting ads in the Muse feed, which is more akin to a newsfeed instead of responses to specific queries, would be a natural way for Meta to test ads on the platform.

stories.title: Perplexity and Intelligence
stories.summary: How perplexity measures progress in AI models, and why it could help developers establish a shared approach to evaluating emerging capabilities.

sources.name: OpenAI
sources.title: Perplexity and Intelligence
sources.text: By Jakub Pachocki, Chief Scientist at OpenAI From afar, it might seem like modern AI is built similarly to how software has been built in previous decades: with a diverse set of techniques targeting specific capabilities. There are indeed a variety of methods, but rather than designing something from scratch, they are mostly harnessing the intelligence coming from a much simpler and less interpretable process: training a compressor (or, equivalently ⁠ (opens in a new window) , predictor) on a very large corpus of data. 1 I believe tracking the pace of progress on training better compressors is key to understanding the arc of advances in AI. In this post, I argue for establishing perplexity (or, equivalently, cross-entropy loss) as a metric to compare between model developers and inform shared safety standards. As a first step, I provide more transparency into pretraining progress at OpenAI. Publishing our internal perplexity measurements took some consideration; it gives competitors a clearer picture of where we stand, but that concern is outweighed by the urgency of establishing shared ⁠ (opens in a new window) safety measures across the industry. We at OpenAI hope for this to be a step towards building a shared scientific basis for future pacing efforts. A simplified, but fundamentally informative, view of AI development is that first, one builds a large computer, then uses it to pretrain a model (compressor) on a large unstructured dataset, then applies a variety of techniques—like prompting, finetuning or reinforcement learning—in different contexts to elicit the latent capabilities of that model. Algorithmic progress can blur the distinction between training phases, but we can still separate the creation of the AI with hard-to-predict emergent capabilities (which I earlier dubbed “ an alien mind ⁠ ”) and the subsequent targeted elicitation. The primary way we measure progress on this key “intelligence substrate” has remained remarkably constant over the years—we have been tracking the perplexity of the models on a held-out dataset. 2 , 3 Perplexity measures how well a model predicts the next token on average; lower perplexity means better predictions. The plot opening this blog post shows how this metric evolved for our models starting with GPT‑3.5. The range of capabilities of models that are largely described by this one metric is stunning. Setting the new perplexity state-of-the-art on older datasets 4 , GPT‑2 was arguably the first model capable of consistently formulating coherent paragraphs of text. The next major leap, GPT‑3, was capable of learning in context, given a few examples of a task. GPT‑3.5, at a log-perplexity of ~0.99 on our current main evaluation dataset, was capable of fluent conversation and formed the basis for the original ChatGPT. GPT‑4, at ~0.91, was proficient at utilizing chain-of-thought reasoning productively, which motivated the subsequent targeted elicitation of this capability and the creation of modern reasoning models. Now, as we have reached losses below 0.8, we have seen the emergence of transformative capabilities in fields like cybersecurity and mathematics. I want to reemphasize that it was not at all clear a priori that these capabilities would appear once those precise perplexity thresholds are met—they can fundamentally be seen as emergent latent capabilities from progress on this one metric. As AI advances very rapidly, the scope and way in which we measure downstream capabilities may change quickly. It would make little sense to evaluate GPT‑2 and GPT‑3 on most modern benchmarks; and the benchmarks used then were largely saturated around GPT‑4. In contrast, I believe looking at progress on pretraining is likely to stay informative. A particular change in the pace of progress comes from the increasing contribution of AI to its own development. The most commonly discussed metrics revolve around AI augmenting and replacing human researchers in all stages of the development cycle; with an ultimate inflection point seen at “full recursive self-improvement”, where the process would be entirely automated with no human oversight. Apart from considering such a state as something we should obviously avoid for the sake of maintaining human control, I find this general framing misses something crucial. There is a potential step change that may come from AI participation in one key part of the development process: algorithmic research on pretraining. We have recently witnessed unprecedented acceleration in another domain. For more than a year, we have been posing open problems in mathematics to our models as one of the ways of evaluating them. Once we upgraded to a model of log-perplexity ~0.76, it started producing groundbreaking results. For many of us that have previously worked in mathematics and adjacent fields, seeing the resolutions to questions we’ve long thought about coming out of the model one after another in a single Slack thread felt deeply surreal. Having experienced that allows us to extrapolate—such a sudden transformation is plausible in deep learning research too. While this field relies more on experimentation, there is a long history of simple insights being missed for years; and so as soon as 2027 we could conceivably see a similar avalanche of fundamental pretraining advancements 5 . While I expect AI will also significantly contribute to progress on alignment and monitoring, I think that progress is unlikely to be fast enough to allow the full potential acceleration in pretraining. Given that the main way new surprising capabilities emerge is by progress on compression, a measure rooted in perplexity could give us a shared benchmark for general intelligence, regardless of the degree of automation of the development process. Extrapolating from recent progress, we should expect further transformative capabilities as we enter the ~0.68-0.7 log-perplexity window. sources.text: Hello and welcome to Eye on AI. In this edition: The biggest news of the week obviously is Nvidia’s decision to rehire Jensen Huang as CEO. My Fortune colleagues and I have been following that story closely and you can find links to our coverage in the “Fortune on AI” section below. The other big story of the week was Anthropic’s IPO, which we also covered in detail. You can find links to some of that coverage in the “Fortune on AI” section too. The latest issue of Fortune magazine also has a great package of stories on the Singularity—what is it, is it here, and what might it mean for business? I wrote the opening essay for that package, which also includes a look at the race to bring brain computer interfaces to market by Emily Forlini and a piece on the debate over whether AI could be conscious by Beatrice Nolan. You can check out the package here . While all the boardroom and stock market drama was playing out this week, a quieter sense of panic has gripped many AI researchers and safety experts. One key reason for their alarm is a report from METR, the nonprofit AI evaluation organization, assessing the extent to which AI is accelerating AI R&D itself at Anthropic. METR estimated that as of October, the pace of AI R&D progress at Anthropic had doubled, and that Anthropic’s use of AI to automate research was likely the major driver of this acceleration. It also said it did not see any reason to prevent further speed ups going forward. Now, METR said it was not entirely confident in its assessment. (It said the true figure could be anywhere from a 30% speedup to a tripling of the pace of research.) But it also revealed that Anthropic had some important restrictions around what METR was allowed to look at as well as what the organization was allowed to publicly disclose. METR was not allowed, for instance, to assess how much computing resources Anthropic was dedicating to AI R&D aimed at improving model capabilities compared to how much it was allocating to R&D aimed at improving AI safety. Also, in the public version of its report, METR was not allowed to publicly disclose Anthropic’s own assessment of how much progress it was making on fundamental algorithmic breakthroughs, as opposed to improvements due to better training methods. AI safety experts were roundly critical of Anthropic for having imposed these restrictions on METR. (The AI safety community has increasingly fallen out of love with Anthropic and increasingly view the company as reckless and hubristic.) Despite these caveats and limitations, METR’s headline figure—a doubling of the pace of AI R&D—has been enough to freak a lot of people out. Many AI experts now think we are approaching “recursive self-improvement” (or RSI), the moment when AI models can autonomously build the next, improved versions of themselves. Many experts think RSI carries a big risk that frontier labs will lose the ability to control models that are being autonomously built at an ever faster rate. If the METR report weren’t enough to frighten people about imminent RSI, Friday brought the news that a mathematician at Anthropic, Levent Alpöge, had used a not-yet-released model to prove the Riemann Hypothesis, considered by many to be the greatest unsolved mathematical problem known to humanity. An AI system that can solve the Riemann Hypothesis, so the logic goes, is also likely to be able to make substantial improvements in the architecture and training of AI models. It was yet another indication that frontier AI labs are on the cusp of RSI. In response, calls for “pacing the frontier” by slowing further progress across all of the frontier AI labs are becoming increasingly urgent. But figuring out how to bring about an industry agreement on slowing down and developing a mechanism for enforcing a slowdown has proved a conundrum. Over the weekend and at least partly in response to the Riemann Hypothesis news, Jakub Pachocki, OpenAI’s chief scientist, wrote a blog post in which he put forth a relatively new idea about how to pace AI progress. In the past, many ideas around governing advanced AI development have focused on the computing power (as measured in FLOPS) used in a model’s training run as a proxy for that model’s capability. But this measure is increasingly seen as too crude. As researchers have developed more efficient AI architectures and training methods, and as they have focused more on data quality and post-training methods such as reinforcement learning, it has been possible to squeeze more capability out of a given amount of base model compute. Reasoning models in particular can exhibit different capabilities depending on how much compute they use at inference as opposed to during training. This all means that a model could have dangerous capabilities and not exceed a particular FLOPS threshold. Pachocki’s idea is to use something called a model’s perplexity as a more direct proxy for capability. Perplexity is a measure of how well a model predicts a data distribution. In the case of a large language model, it is how well it predicts the next token (the next word or part of a word) in a sentence. The lower the perplexity, the better the model is at this task. Pachocki notes that as AI models have gotten better at predicting the next word in a sentence, they have also gotten better at other tasks. So perplexity is a not terrible proxy for a model’s overall capabilities. Pachocki’s blog has gotten a lot of attention for publishing a graph that reveals the perplexity measurements of many of OpenAI’s models. He writes the GPT-3.5, which was the base model for the original version of ChatGPT in late 2022, had a log perplexity score just a hair below 1. It could string together a lot of coherent dialogue, but it was not capable at many other things, and was notably bad at mathematics. sources.text: President Donald Trump said Monday that he personally intervened to secure Jensen Huang ’s return as Nvidia CEO, telling CNBC that he spoke with the chipmaker’s board before it reversed course and reinstated its co-founder. “I made the deal,” Trump told CNBC’s Eamon Javers during an interview on “Squawk on the Street.” Trump described his involvement in the decision, which came less than two weeks after Huang resigned, and addressed questions about national security concerns surrounding the Nvidia executive's return.
